platforms.title: Is It PMS, or Could It Be PMDD?
platforms.meta_description: Mood swings before your period severe enough to disrupt work or relationships? How ACOG tells PMS apart from PMDD, and what treatment actually helps.
platforms.body_html:
Assumed mood swings before your period are just something everyone deals with, but the severity is bad enough to disrupt work or your relationships? The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) explains that PMS and PMDD differ in both severity and the underlying mechanism, not just intensity of the same thing. Simply pushing through it every month can mean missing treatment that's actually available.

Why the severity is so different

PMS shows up as mild to moderate physical and emotional symptoms during the luteal phase after ovulation — bloating, breast tenderness, and a bit of irritability are typical. Daily functioning isn't seriously disrupted.

PMDD comes from a completely different mechanism. According to the International Association for Premenstrual Disorders (IAPMD), the normal hormonal fluctuation itself isn't the problem — the brain's serotonin regulation system reacts unusually strongly to that fluctuation, producing severe anger, depression, anxiety, or sudden mood swings. These symptoms are intense enough to genuinely interfere with work performance or family relationships.

How to tell them apart, and what to check

First, whether the symptoms actually cause missed workdays or conflict in relationships. PMS is uncomfortable but manageable, while PMDD is severe enough to noticeably disrupt daily functioning.

Second, whether the symptoms clearly ease within a few days of the period starting. ACOG considers tracking symptoms on a calendar across at least two menstrual cycles central to diagnosis, confirming they cluster in the luteal phase and improve within days of bleeding starting. If mood symptoms continue all month long, it may not be PMDD at all but rather an existing mood disorder that simply worsens premenstrually.

What matters most is not relying solely on supplements or self-treatment if the symptoms are severe. International guidelines list selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) as a first-line treatment with proven effectiveness for PMDD, whether taken continuously or only during the luteal phase. If symptoms are severe enough to include thoughts of self-harm, reaching out to a doctor right away is essential.

PMDD's diagnostic criteria also include physical and behavioral signs beyond mood — noticeable fatigue, disrupted sleep, appetite changes or specific food cravings, and a sense of feeling overwhelmed or out of control. Having several of these show up together with the mood symptoms, rather than just one on its own, makes PMDD more likely than ordinary PMS.

A simple way to track this is rating mood and physical symptoms on a 1-to-10 scale each day for two cycles, rather than just noting whether symptoms appeared at all. That kind of scored log makes the luteal-phase pattern, and how sharply it drops off after the period starts, much easier for both you and a doctor to see clearly.

To recap: bloating and mild irritability point toward ordinary PMS, while severe anger, depression, or anxiety that repeats specifically during the luteal phase and disrupts work or relationships points toward PMDD. Tracking symptoms for about two cycles and bringing that record to an OB-GYN makes a real difference in getting an accurate diagnosis and the right treatment plan.
